title: Basic Applications of Differential and Integral Calculus in Business and Economics
outcomes: Explain the derivative as a rate of change and find it from the first principle for simple functions.
Differentiate using standard results and the sum, product, quotient and chain rules, including implicit, parametric and logarithmic differentiation and second-order derivatives.
Interpret the derivative as the gradient of a curve and use first and second derivatives to locate maxima and minima.
Apply derivatives to cost, revenue and profit: average and marginal cost, marginal revenue, break-even, profit maximisation, MPC and MPS.
Integrate using standard formulae, substitution, partial fractions and integration by parts; evaluate definite integrals and use their properties.
Recover total cost and total revenue (and demand) from marginal functions.

meta.exam_tip: Questions are formula-driven: learn the standard derivative and integral tables cold. In applications, write the function you are differentiating (R, C or P) before you differentiate — most errors come from differentiating the wrong one.

concepts.title: The derivative and the first principle
body: If y = f(x) and x changes by a small amount h, y changes by f(x + h) − f(x). The average rate of change is [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h. Its limit as h → 0 is the derivative, written dy/dx, f′(x) or d/dx f(x) (also called the differential coefficient).
Finding the derivative straight from this limit is called differentiation from the first principle (ab initio). Example: for f(x) = x², [(x + h)² − x²]/h = 2x + h → 2x.
f is differentiable at x = c if this limit exists there. A function that is differentiable at a point is continuous there (the converse is not always true).
concepts.analogy: A car's speedometer shows the derivative of distance with respect to time — the rate at this instant, not the average for the whole trip.
concepts.work: Every "marginal" figure in economics and costing — marginal cost, marginal revenue, marginal propensity to consume — is a derivative.

concepts.title: Standard derivatives
body: d/dx (xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹ (any real n); d/dx (k) = 0 for a constant k.
d/dx (eˣ) = eˣ; d/dx (eᵃˣ) = a eᵃˣ; d/dx (aˣ) = aˣ logₑa; d/dx (logₑx) = 1/x.
d/dx [k f(x)] = k f′(x) — constants come out of the derivative.
concepts.analogy: The table is your multiplication table for calculus — you should not have to work these out in the exam hall.
concepts.work: Spreadsheet growth models use eˣ and aˣ; knowing their rates of change lets you sanity-check a model's marginal figures.

concepts.title: Rules of differentiation
body: Sum/difference: (f ± g)′ = f′ ± g′.
Product rule: (fg)′ = f g′ + g f′ — "first × derivative of second + second × derivative of first".
Quotient rule: (f/g)′ = (g f′ − f g′)/g², g ≠ 0 — "denominator × derivative of numerator − numerator × derivative of denominator, over denominator squared".
Chain rule (function of a function): if y = f(z) and z = g(x), then dy/dx = (dy/dz)(dz/dx). Example: d/dx (3x² + 1)⁵ = 5(3x² + 1)⁴ × 6x.
concepts.analogy: The chain rule is a gear train: if the first gear turns 3 times for each turn of the second, and the second 4 times for each turn of the third, the first turns 12 times per turn of the third.
concepts.work: Revenue = price × quantity, and both may depend on output — the product rule is how marginal revenue is derived from a demand curve.

concepts.title: Implicit, parametric and logarithmic differentiation
body: Implicit: when y is mixed with x in an equation f(x, y) = 0, differentiate every term with respect to x, writing dy/dx wherever y is differentiated (d/dx of y² is 2y dy/dx), then solve for dy/dx.
Parametric: if x = f(t) and y = h(t), then dy/dx = (dy/dt) ÷ (dx/dt), provided dx/dt ≠ 0.

Logarithmic: for products of many factors or variable powers such as xˣ, take logₑ of both sides first, differentiate, then multiply back by y. For y = xˣ: logₑy = x logₑx → (1/y) dy/dx = 1 + logₑx → dy/dx = xˣ(1 + logₑx).
concepts.analogy: Taking logs first is like converting a multiplication problem into an addition problem before you start — the work becomes simpler.
concepts.work: Growth-rate analysis (the percentage change of a product of factors) uses logarithmic differentiation: the growth rate of revenue ≈ growth rate of price + growth rate of quantity.

concepts.title: Second derivative and the gradient of a curve
body: Differentiating f′(x) again gives the second derivative d²y/dx² = f″(x); further differentiation gives f‴(x), and so on.

Geometrically, f′(a) is the gradient of the curve y = f(x) at the point where x = a — the steepness of the line that just touches the curve there. Positive gradient → the curve is rising; negative → falling; zero → a stationary point.
At a stationary point (f′(a) = 0): f″(a) < 0 → local maximum; f″(a) > 0 → local minimum.
concepts.analogy: On a road, the first derivative tells you whether you are going uphill or downhill; the second tells you whether the slope is getting steeper or flattening out — at the top of a hill it flattens and then turns down.
concepts.work: Finding the output that maximises profit or minimises average cost is a stationary-point problem checked with the second derivative.

concepts.title: Applications: cost, revenue, profit, break-even and propensities
body: Total cost C(x) = fixed cost + variable cost. Average cost AC = C(x)/x; AVC = V(x)/x; AFC = F/x. Marginal cost MC = dC/dx — approximately the cost of one more unit.
Revenue R(x) = p × x (p from the demand function). Marginal revenue MR = dR/dx. Profit P(x) = R(x) − C(x); marginal profit = dP/dx.
Break-even point: R(x) = C(x) (no profit, no loss). Profit maximum: dP/dx = 0, i.e. MR = MC, with d²P/dx² < 0. Average cost is least where AC′ = 0, and at that output AC = MC.
Consumption function C = f(Y): marginal propensity to consume MPC = dC/dY. Saving S = Y − C, so MPS = dS/dY = 1 − MPC.
concepts.analogy: Marginal cost is the price of the next slice of pizza you order; average cost is the bill divided by the slices already eaten.
concepts.work: Pricing studies, make-or-buy decisions and break-even analysis in cost accounting all use these definitions — the calculus version just gives exact answers for curved cost and demand functions.

concepts.title: Integration — the reverse of differentiation
body: If d/dx F(x) = f(x), then ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + c. The arbitrary constant c is the constant of integration, because constants vanish on differentiation.
Standard results: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c (n ≠ −1); ∫ (1/x) dx = logₑ|x| + c; ∫ eˣ dx = eˣ + c; ∫ eᵃˣ dx = eᵃˣ/a + c; ∫ aˣ dx = aˣ/logₑa + c; ∫ k dx = kx + c.
Rules: ∫ k f(x) dx = k ∫ f(x) dx; ∫ [f(x) ± g(x)] dx = ∫ f dx ± ∫ g dx. There is no general product or quotient rule — use the methods below.
concepts.analogy: Differentiation turns a recipe into a list of ingredients per minute; integration rebuilds the recipe — but cannot tell how much was already in the pot (that is the + c).
concepts.work: Totals from rates — total cost from marginal cost, total revenue from marginal revenue — are integrals.

concepts.title: Methods of integration
body: Substitution: if the integrand contains a function and its derivative, put t = that function. ∫ (2x + 3)⁴ dx: t = 2x + 3, dx = dt/2 → (2x + 3)⁵/10 + c. Special case — when the numerator is the derivative of the denominator, the answer is the log of the denominator: logₑ|f(x)| + c is the integral of f′(x)/f(x).
Integration by parts: ∫ u v dx = u ∫ v dx − ∫ [u′ ∫ v dx] dx. Choose u as the factor that becomes simpler on differentiation (e.g. x in x eˣ).
Partial fractions: split a proper rational function into simpler fractions. (x + 5)/[(x + 1)(x + 2)] = 4/(x + 1) − 3/(x + 2).

Standard forms: ∫ dx/(x² − a²) = (1/2a) logₑ|(x − a)/(x + a)| + c; ∫ dx/(a² − x²) = (1/2a) logₑ|(a + x)/(a − x)| + c; ∫ dx/√(x² + a²) = logₑ|x + √(x² + a²)| + c; ∫ dx/√(x² − a²) = logₑ|x + √(x² − a²)| + c.
concepts.analogy: Substitution is renaming a messy part so the integral looks like one from the table; by parts is trading a hard integral for an easier one.
concepts.work: These methods matter less in practice (software integrates) than in the exam — but recognising f′/f patterns gives instant answers in MCQs.

concepts.title: Definite integrals and their properties
body: If F′ = f, then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a). The constant of integration cancels, so it is not written. a is the lower limit, b the upper limit.

Properties: (I) the variable is a dummy — ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(t) dt; (II) ∫ₐᵇ f = −∫ᵦᵃ f (reversing limits changes sign); (III) ∫ₐᵇ f = ∫ₐᶜ f + ∫ᶜᵇ f; (IV) ∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x) dx; (V) if f(a + x) = f(x), then ∫₀ⁿᵃ f = n ∫₀ᵃ f; (VI) ∫₋ₐᵃ f = 2∫₀ᵃ f if f is even (f(−x) = f(x)) and 0 if f is odd (f(−x) = −f(x)).
For a curve above the x-axis, ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx is the area between the curve, the x-axis and the lines x = a, x = b.
concepts.analogy: A definite integral is a meter reading: the total between two readings is "closing minus opening" — the starting point of the meter (the constant) does not matter.
concepts.work: Total extra cost of raising production from one level to another is a definite integral of marginal cost between the two outputs.

concepts.title: From marginal functions back to totals
body: Total cost: C(x) = ∫ MC dx + k, where k is found from a known value — usually the fixed cost, since C(0) = fixed cost.
Total revenue: R(x) = ∫ MR dx + k, with k = 0 because nothing sold means no revenue (R(0) = 0). The demand (average revenue) function is p = R(x)/x.
The change in total cost (or revenue) between outputs a and b is ∫ₐᵇ MC dx (or ∫ₐᵇ MR dx) — fixed cost does not affect it.
Similarly, a curve can be found from its slope: if dy/dx is known and the curve passes through a given point, integrate and use the point to fix c.
concepts.analogy: Knowing how much fuel a car burns per kilometre at each speed (marginal) lets you work out the fuel for the whole trip (total) — but you need the starting fuel level (the constant) to know what is left in the tank.
concepts.work: Budgeting for an expansion: "what will the extra 10 units cost?" is ∫ MC between the two output levels — exactly what a cost accountant prepares for a capacity decision.

illustrations.title: Derivatives from the first principle
illustrations.q: Using the first principle, differentiate (a) f(x) = 3x² + 2x and (b) f(x) = 1/x (x ≠ 0). Evaluate each at x = 2.

solution.text: (a) f(x + h) − f(x) = 3(x + h)² + 2(x + h) − 3x² − 2x = 6xh + 3h² + 2h. Dividing by h: 6x + 3h + 2 → 6x + 2 as h → 0. At x = 2: 14.
(b) f(x + h) − f(x) = 1/(x + h) − 1/x = −h/[x(x + h)]. Dividing by h: −1/[x(x + h)] → −1/x². At x = 2: −1/4.

illustrations.title: Using the rules: sum, product, quotient, chain
illustrations.q: Differentiate with respect to x: (a) 4x³ − 5x² + 7x − 9; (b) x²eˣ; (c) (2x + 3)/(x − 1); (d) (3x² + 1)⁵; (e) logₑ(x² + 4).

illustrations.title: Implicit, parametric and logarithmic differentiation
illustrations.q: (a) Find dy/dx for x² + y² = 25 and its value at (3, 4). (b) If x = 2t² and y = 4t, find dy/dx. (c) Differentiate y = xˣ.

solution.text: (a) Differentiate term by term: 2x + 2y dy/dx = 0 → dy/dx = −x/y. At (3, 4): −3/4.
(b) dx/dt = 4t, dy/dt = 4 → dy/dx = 4/(4t) = 1/t. (At t = 2 the slope is 1/2.)
(c) logₑy = x logₑx. Differentiating: (1/y) dy/dx = x × (1/x) + logₑx = 1 + logₑx, so dy/dx = xˣ(1 + logₑx). At x = 2 this is about 4 × 1.6931 = 6.77.

checks.label: dy/dx = 1/t at t = 2 for x = 2t², y = 4t
derivative of xˣ at x = 2 ≈ 4(1 + logₑ2)

illustrations.title: Gradient, second derivative, maximum and minimum
illustrations.q: For y = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 4, find the gradient at x = 0, the stationary points, and decide whether each is a maximum or a minimum.

solution.text: dy/dx = 3x² − 12x + 9; at x = 0 the gradient is 9.
Stationary points: 3(x² − 4x + 3) = 0 → x = 1 or x = 3. d²y/dx² = 6x − 12.

illustrations.title: Least average cost and maximum profit
illustrations.q: A firm's total cost is C(x) = 2x² + 40x + 5,000 and its demand function is p = 400 − 3x (₹). Find (a) the output at which average cost is least and show that AC = MC there; (b) the profit-maximising output, price and profit, and verify MR = MC.

solution.title: (a) Average cost
solution.text: AC = 2x + 40 + 5000/x; d(AC)/dx = 2 − 5000/x² = 0 → x² = 2500 → x = 50. Second derivative 10000/x³ > 0 → minimum. Least AC = 100 + 40 + 100 = ₹240. MC = 4x + 40 = ₹240 at x = 50 — equal to AC.
Check: MR = 400 − 6x = 184 and MC = 4x + 40 = 184 at x = 36 — MR = MC, as theory says.

illustrations.title: Break-even point
illustrations.q: A start-up making smart meters has fixed costs of ₹3,60,000. Each meter costs ₹450 to make and sells for ₹750. Find the cost and revenue functions, the break-even output, and the profit if 1,500 meters are sold.

head: Integrand
Method

solution.text: Check any answer by differentiating it — you should get the integrand back.

illustrations.title: Definite integrals, properties and area
illustrations.q: Evaluate (a) ∫₁³ (3x² + 2x) dx; (b) ∫₀² x² dx; (c) ∫₋₂² x³ dx; (d) ∫₋₁¹ x² dx. (e) Find the area enclosed by y = 4x − x² and the x-axis.

solution.text: (c) x³ is odd, so the integral over [−2, 2] is 0. (Directly: [x⁴/4] = 4 − 4 = 0.)
(d) x² is even: 2∫₀¹ x² dx = 2 × 1/3 = 2/3.
(e) The curve meets the x-axis at x = 0 and x = 4 and is above it in between. Area = [2x² − x³/3]₀⁴ = 32 − 64/3 = 32/3 ≈ 10.67 square units.

checks.label: area under y = 4x − x² from 0 to 4

illustrations.title: Total cost and demand from marginal functions
illustrations.q: (a) MC = 3x² − 12x + 40 and fixed cost is ₹500. Find the total and average cost functions, the cost of 10 units, and the extra cost of raising output from 4 to 8 units. (b) MR = 100 − 4x. Find the total revenue and demand functions.

solution.text: Extra cost = ∫₄⁸ MC dx = [x³ − 6x² + 40x]₄⁸ = 448 − 128 = ₹320 (fixed cost plays no part).

checks.label: extra cost when output rises from 4 to 8

jobs.title: Advising a manufacturer on price
jobs.role: Cost and management accountant at a mid-sized factory
jobs.situation: Marketing estimates that the price at which x units a week can be sold is p = 700 − 2x. Costing gives C(x) = x² + 100x + 15,000 a week. The owner wants to know the best output and price.
steps: Revenue R = 700x − 2x²; profit P = R − C = 600x − 3x² − 15,000.
dP/dx = 600 − 6x = 0 → x = 100 units; d²P/dx² = −6 < 0, so this is a maximum.
Present the answer with a sensitivity note: the result is only as good as the demand and cost estimates.
jobs.takeaway: Set MR = MC (equivalently dP/dx = 0) and confirm with the second derivative — the same steps as in the exam.

jobs.title: Budgeting the cost of extra capacity
jobs.role: Finance executive preparing a capacity-expansion note
jobs.situation: The plant currently makes 20 machines a month. Engineering gives marginal cost as MC = 2x + 50 (₹ thousand per machine). Management asks what it would cost to raise output to 30 machines.
steps: The extra cost is the area under the MC curve between 20 and 30: ∫₂₀³⁰ (2x + 50) dx.
Fixed costs do not enter, because they do not change with output — mention this explicitly in the note.
jobs.takeaway: A definite integral of a marginal function gives the change in the total — a direct budgeting tool.
jobs.think: If the consumption function of a household is C = 2,000 + 0.75Y, what are its MPC and MPS?

checks.label: extra cost (₹ thousand) from 20 to 30 units with MC = 2x + 50

mcqs.q: The gradient (slope of the tangent) of the curve y = x³ − 4x² + 7x − 2 at x = 2 is:
mcqs.explain: dy/dx = 3x² − 8x + 7 = 12 − 16 + 7 = 3. 4 is the value of y at x = 2, not the slope.

mcqs.q: d/dx (e⁴ˣ) equals:
mcqs.explain: d/dx (eᵃˣ) = a eᵃˣ. Treating eˣ like a power xⁿ gives the wrong last option.

mcqs.q: d/dx (5ˣ) equals:
mcqs.explain: d/dx (aˣ) = aˣ logₑa. The power rule applies only when the variable is in the base.

mcqs.q: The derivative of x³ logₑx is:
mcqs.explain: Product rule: x³ × 1/x + logₑx × 3x² = x² + 3x² logₑx = x²(1 + 3 logₑx).

mcqs.q: d/dx [x/(x + 1)] equals:
mcqs.explain: Quotient rule: [(x + 1)(1) − x(1)]/(x + 1)² = 1/(x + 1)².

mcqs.q: d/dx (2x + 1)⁶ equals:
mcqs.explain: Chain rule: 6(2x + 1)⁵ × d/dx(2x + 1) = 12(2x + 1)⁵. Forgetting the inner derivative gives 6(2x + 1)⁵.

mcqs.q: If y = eˣ + e⁻ˣ, then d²y/dx² equals:
mcqs.explain: y′ = eˣ − e⁻ˣ, y″ = eˣ + e⁻ˣ = y. (eˣ − e⁻ˣ is only the first derivative.)

mcqs.q: The value of the second derivative of y = x⁴ at x = 1 is:
mcqs.explain: y′ = 4x³, y″ = 12x², which is 12 at x = 1.

mcqs.q: If xy = 16, then dy/dx equals:
mcqs.explain: Differentiate implicitly: x dy/dx + y = 0 → dy/dx = −y/x (= −16/x²).

mcqs.q: If x = t² and y = t³, then dy/dx equals:
mcqs.explain: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = 3t²/(2t) = 3t/2.

mcqs.q: The total cost of x units is C = 0.02x³ − 0.5x² + 10x + 200. The marginal cost at x = 10 is:
mcqs.explain: MC = 0.06x² − x + 10 = 6 − 10 + 10 = 6. 270 is the total cost of 10 units — do not confuse total with marginal; 16 forgets the −x term.

mcqs.q: Total revenue is R = 50x − 0.5x². Marginal revenue at x = 20 is:
mcqs.explain: MR = 50 − x = 30. 800 is total revenue at 20 units.

mcqs.q: Fixed cost ₹2,40,000, variable cost ₹60 per unit, selling price ₹100 per unit. The break-even output is:
mcqs.explain: At break-even R = C: 100x = 2,40,000 + 60x → x = 2,40,000/40 = 6,000. Dividing by 60 or by 100 is the usual slip.

mcqs.q: Profit is P(x) = −2x² + 120x − 500. Profit is maximum at x =
mcqs.explain: P′ = −4x + 120 = 0 → x = 30; P″ = −4 < 0 confirms a maximum.

mcqs.q: Total cost is C = x² + 16 (x units). Average cost is least at x =
mcqs.explain: AC = x + 16/x; AC′ = 1 − 16/x² = 0 → x = 4 (least AC = 8).

mcqs.q: The consumption function is C = 400 + 0.7Y. The marginal propensity to save is:
mcqs.explain: MPC = dC/dY = 0.7. Since Y = C + S, MPS = 1 − MPC = 0.3.

mcqs.q: ∫ x⁴ dx equals:
mcqs.explain: Raise the power by one and divide by the new power. 4x³ is the derivative, not the integral.

mcqs.q: ∫ (1/x) dx equals:
mcqs.explain: The power formula fails for n = −1; the integral of 1/x is logₑ|x| + c.

mcqs.q: ∫ e³ˣ dx equals:
mcqs.explain: ∫ eᵃˣ dx = eᵃˣ/a + c — divide by a when integrating, multiply when differentiating.

mcqs.q: ∫₀² (3x² + 1) dx equals:
∫₁⁴ √x dx equals:
∫₋₃³ x⁵ dx equals:
mcqs.explain: x⁵ is an odd function (f(−x) = −f(x)), so its integral over [−a, a] is 0.

mcqs.q: ∫ x eˣ dx equals:
mcqs.explain: By parts with u = x: x eˣ − ∫ eˣ dx = eˣ(x − 1) + c.

mcqs.q: Marginal cost is MC = 2x + 5 and fixed cost is ₹100. The total cost of 10 units is:
mcqs.explain: TC = x² + 5x + 100 (the constant of integration is the fixed cost). At x = 10: 100 + 50 + 100 = ₹250.

mcqs.q: Marginal revenue is MR = 40 − 2x. The demand (price) function is:
mcqs.explain: R = ∫ MR dx = 40x − x² (no constant, since R = 0 when x = 0). p = R/x = 40 − x.

mcqs.q: ∫ 2x/(x² + 1) dx equals:
mcqs.explain: Substitute t = x² + 1, dt = 2x dx: ∫ dt/t = logₑ t + c.

mcqs.q: Using the first principle, the derivative of a constant function f(x) = k is:
mcqs.explain: f(x + h) − f(x) = k − k = 0 for every h, so the limit of 0/h is 0.

mcqs.q: The maximum value of y = −x² + 6x + 5 is:
mcqs.explain: y′ = −2x + 6 = 0 → x = 3; y″ = −2 < 0. y(3) = −9 + 18 + 5 = 14. (3 is where the maximum occurs, not its value.)

mcqs.q: MC = 4x + 10. The increase in total cost when output rises from 10 to 20 units is:
At the output where profit is maximum (with the second-order condition met):
mcqs.explain: P′ = R′ − C′ = 0 gives MR = MC. TR = TC is break-even; AC = MC marks the least average cost.

questions.q: Differentiate (a) y = (x² + 1)(3x − 2) and find its value at x = 1; (b) y = (3x + 2)/(2x − 1); (c) y = e^(x²).

scheme.pt: (a) Product rule applied and simplified to 9x² − 4x + 3
(b) Quotient rule with correct order of terms; −7/(2x − 1)²

remarks: Reversing the order in the quotient-rule numerator flips the sign — a very common slip.
Candidates who expand (a) first and differentiate the cubic also score full marks.
mistakes: Differentiating a product as the product of derivatives.
tips: Write "u = …, v = …" before applying the product or quotient rule.
Simplify the numerator fully — examiners award a mark for the final simplified form.

questions.q: The total cost of producing x units is C(x) = 0.5x² + 30x + 1,800 and the demand function is p = 150 − x (₹). Find (a) the output that maximises profit, the price and the maximum profit; (b) the output at which average cost is least, the least average cost, and show that MC equals AC at that output.

model.text: (b) AC = 0.5x + 30 + 1,800/x. d(AC)/dx = 0.5 − 1,800/x² = 0 → x² = 3,600 → x = 60. Second derivative 3,600/x³ > 0 → minimum. Least AC = 30 + 30 + 30 = ₹90. MC = x + 30 = ₹90 at x = 60 = AC.

scheme.pt: AC minimised at x = 60 with second-order check; least AC ₹90

remarks: Many candidates maximise revenue instead of profit — read which function is to be optimised.
Marks are reserved for the second-order condition; do not skip it.
mistakes: Minimising total cost instead of average cost.
tips: State the economic interpretation in one line at the end.

questions.q: (a) Evaluate ∫ (4x³ − 6x + 2/x) dx. (b) Using a property of definite integrals, evaluate ∫₀¹ x(1 − x)⁴ dx. (c) Marginal cost is MC = 3x² − 8x + 10 and fixed cost is ₹60. Find the total cost function and the total and average cost of 6 units.

model.text: (b) By ∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x) dx with a = 1: ∫₀¹ (1 − x)x⁴ dx = ∫₀¹ (x⁴ − x⁵) dx = 1/5 − 1/6 = 1/30 (≈ 0.03).

scheme.pt: (a) Each term integrated, log term and constant included
(b) Property f(a − x) applied to simplify
(c) Constant of integration = fixed cost; TC function

remarks: In (b), expanding (1 − x)⁴ works but takes much longer — the property is what the examiner is testing.
Several answers drop the constant in (c), giving TC ₹132.
tips: Write the property you use in symbols before applying it.
Always add "+ c" to indefinite integrals.

summary: dy/dx = lim [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h as h → 0 — rate of change, slope of the tangent.
xⁿ → nxⁿ⁻¹; eᵃˣ → a eᵃˣ; aˣ → aˣ logₑa; logₑx → 1/x; constant → 0.
Product (uv)′ = uv′ + vu′; quotient (u/v)′ = (vu′ − uv′)/v²; chain dy/dx = dy/dz · dz/dx.
Implicit: differentiate both sides; parametric: (dy/dt)/(dx/dt); logarithmic for xˣ and long products.
MC = dC/dx; MR = dR/dx; profit max MR = MC; break-even R = C; least AC where AC = MC; MPC + MPS = 1.

viva.q: What is a derivative, and what does finding it from the first principle mean?
viva.model: The derivative of y equals f of x is the limit of the ratio of the change in f of x to the small change h in x, as h tends to zero. It measures the instantaneous rate of change of y with respect to x, and geometrically the slope of the tangent. Finding it from the first principle means computing this limit, f of x plus h minus f of x over h, directly from the definition instead of using formulas.

viva.q: State the product rule and the quotient rule of differentiation.
viva.model: The product rule says the derivative of u times v is u times the derivative of v plus v times the derivative of u. The quotient rule says the derivative of u over v is v times the derivative of u minus u times the derivative of v, all divided by v squared, provided v is not zero.

viva.q: How do you find a maximum or minimum using derivatives, and what is the condition for maximum profit?
viva.model: First put the first derivative equal to zero and solve for x to get the stationary points. Then check the second derivative: if it is negative the point is a maximum, and if it is positive the point is a minimum. Profit is maximum where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, with the second derivative of profit negative.

viva.q: Why do we add a constant in an indefinite integral but not in a definite integral?
viva.model: Integration is the reverse of differentiation, and since the derivative of any constant is zero, many functions differing only by a constant have the same derivative, so we add an arbitrary constant c to an indefinite integral. In a definite integral we take F of b minus F of a, so the constant cancels out and is not written.
